title: Class 11 Chemistry — Chemical Equilibrium Study Guide
notes: Equilibrium occurs when opposing processes have equal rates, so macroscopic properties remain constant. Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. A closed system at constant conditions is needed for stable equilibrium composition.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations and omitting pure solids and liquids. A large K means products are favored at equilibrium; a small K means reactants are favored. K describes position, not speed. At fixed temperature, changing concentration or pressure may shift composition but does not change K; temperature changes K.
For gaseous equilibria Kp uses partial pressures. Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is gaseous product coefficients minus gaseous reactant coefficients. Omit solids and liquids from Δn; if Δn = 0, Kp = Kc.

Le Chatelier's principle: a system shifts to partially oppose a disturbance. Adding reactant or removing product generally favors products; adding product or removing reactant favors reactants. Increasing pressure by decreasing volume favors the side with fewer gas moles; equal gas counts give no pressure shift. Raising temperature favors the endothermic direction and changes K; lowering temperature favors the exothermic direction. A catalyst speeds both directions and reaches equilibrium sooner but changes neither K nor equilibrium composition. Numerical calculations are not required in this unit.

Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat has four gas moles on the left and two on the right. Higher pressure shifts toward NH₃. Higher temperature shifts toward N₂ and H₂ because the forward reaction is exothermic. A catalyst changes rate, not position.
formulas: Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b) for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD
Δn = gaseous product coefficients − gaseous reactant coefficients
keyPoints: Equilibrium is dynamic; forward and reverse rates are equal, not zero.
Use equilibrium concentrations; omit pure solids and liquids from K expressions.
K is temperature-dependent; catalysts do not change K.
Pressure favors fewer gas moles only when the sides have different gas counts.
Increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction.
practiceQuestions: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), predict the effect of increased pressure and explain.
For an exothermic forward reaction, predict effects of higher temperature and a catalyst.
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), determine Δn and relate Kp to Kc.
summary: Equilibrium constants describe composition at dynamic equilibrium. Use stoichiometric powers, count only gaseous species in Δn and apply Le Chatelier by identifying which disturbance the system partially opposes.
